[[RunningHead]]

A Body-Centered Mind

Freud's More Radical Idea

Irene Fast PHD

Irene Fast

337 Lake Park Lane
Ann Arbor, MI 48103

Irene Fast  

Freud proposed two sharply contrasting conceptions of the body's place in mental structure. Both were radical departures from established views of the mind. In the first, body-based thought is rooted in the drives and instincts. It is primitive in contrast to the body-free, logical, and rational thought of maturity. Freud remained committed to this view in his formal conceptions of the mind throughout his working life. It remains the one most fully accepted in psychoanalytic thought today.

Less formally, particularly in conceptions of the “accidental” factors that structure the primary processes, “stereotype plates” that pattern our experience, thinking as “action in the mind,” and “internalizations” that form our inner worlds, he suggested an even more radical notion. In this view, “bodily” refers to the behavioral patterns (of personal motivation, action, attitude, wish, and feeling) as opposed to mental ones. Body-based patterns occur primitively, but they may also become mental and structure the mind at the highest levels of sophistication. Neither in Freud's time nor subsequently, however, has it been possible to integrate this second view of the bodily in mental functioning into the accepted psychoanalytic theory of mind.

Now, however, developing perspectives in psychoanalysis provide a framework in which this second view can be accommodated. In this model the mind is initially composed of social-emotional-behavioral patterns (in Stern's useful term, “patterns of lived experience”) established in familial life (Freud's “accidental” factors that form “stereotype plates”). These patterns, articulated and modified in the course of development, can increasingly be activated mentally with or without accompanying bodily action (Freud's “action in the mind” and “internalization”). These, rather than the rational-logical processes of traditional thought, constitute the mature mind.

The Relational Unconscious, The Enchanted Interior, and the Return of the Repressed**

Jeremy Safran PHD

Jeremy Safran

65 Fifth Avenue
New York, NY 10003
safranj@newschool.edu

Jeremy Safran  

In recent years, a number of relationally oriented psychoanalysts have begun to think of the unconscious as generative and creative, rather than as a seething cauldron of potentially dangerous distinctive drives. There is also a tendency to view the unconscious in mystical or spiritual terms. For these theorists the emphasis tends to be on infusing life with the vitality of the unconscious or on being guided by the unconscious forces rather than on taming and modulating them. In this article I argue that this perspective on the unconscious is consistent with a world view that is characteristically American and that it has its roots in developments within both popular and academic psychology that preceded the absorption of psychoanalysis by American culture. I also argue that it is consistent with certain culturally specific features of the American Protestant tradition that began emerging in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries and that have had an important impact on contemporary American culture and on popular psychology. Finally I speculate about the role that the tension between secular and religious (or rational versus mystical) world views play in the evolution of psychoanalytic theory.

Clinical Implications of Biographic Disclosure*

Sophia Richman PHD ABPP

303 Second Avenue, Suite 5
New York, NY 10003

Sophia Richman  

memoir, biographic, self-disclosure, hidden, transference, vulnerable, subjectivity

The author, a child survivor of the Nazi Holocaust, wrote a memoir that was published in January 2002. This paper examines the effects of biographic self-disclosure on the analytic dyad and the treatment process. The complex subject of self-disclosure has received much attention in recent years, but little has been written about what happens to the treatment when patients learn details about the private life of the analyst. Recently, several biographical accounts have appeared in the literature, and the internet has made certain biographical information readily available to patients, yet there is little, if any, data about the impact of these disclosures. In this paper, the author describes the personal and professional experiences that influenced her attitude toward self-disclosure and led to her decision to write a memoir. Several clinical vignettes illustrate the complex reactions of patients to the disclosure as it came up in the treatment. Various issues explored include the impact on the transference, potential problems such as intrusion of the analyst's subjectivity into the analytic space, and analyst vulnerability, as well as benefits such as an atmosphere of heightened emotional intensity and intimacy which ultimately enriches the analytic work.

Implications for Supervision and Self-Supervision*

Amy Schaffer PHD

Amy Schaffer

545 West End Avenue, 11D
New York, NY 10024

Amy Schaffer  

supervision, self-supervision, training, psychoanalysis, self-analysis, curative fantasy, therapeutic action.

The analyst embarking on training often harbors strong, unconscious convictions about the nature of cure. The sense of what is curative may have multiple derivations and is often closely related to unconscious motivations for entering the field. These curative fantasies often endure, dismantled by neither the analyst's own analysis nor by training. Instead, they persist and influence clinical choice. Maturation as an analyst therefore requires a self-supervisory grappling with the differences between what feels curative and publicly held theories of therapeutic action. Supervision should recognize the strength of the analyst's curative leanings and should foster the self-supervision requisite for the analyst to know and gradually transform them.

Vicissitudes of Authenticity in the Psychoanalytic Situation**

M. Thompson PHD

M. Thompson

684 Colusa Avenue
Berkeley, CA 94707

M. Thompson  

The author argues that the dynamics of the analytic relationship are rooted in a capacity for authenticity that is reflected in the manner by which analyst and patient alike typically depict the analytic experience. Relying on the existential views of Nietzsche and Heidegger, the author conceives the authentic sensibility as the acceptance of sacrifice and delayed gratification in the mutual pursuit of a working relationship devoted to personal integrity and self-awareness. The article focuses specifically on the relation between authenticity and Freud's conception of free association and neutrality; Winnicott's explication of the therapeutic component of suffering; Bion's critique of psychic freedom; Lacan's treatment of the cure; and the relation between authenticity and the extra-transference dimension of the analyst-patient dynamic.

The Dialectics of Analytic Disclosure

Discussion of Barbara Pizer's Paper

Hazel Ipp PHD

Hazel Ipp

12 Lawton Boulevard
3d Floor
Toronto, Ontario M4V 1Z4
Canada

Hazel Ipp  

Barbara Pizer, in her wonderfully explicit and scrupulous unpacking of a disclosure, directs us to a place of contemplative reflection and self-scrutiny as we consider choices made and not made in our own struggles with ourselves and those we seek to help within the inevitably fateful mix of subjectivities unleashed in the crucible of our work.

In keeping with her other papers that directly or indirectly address the still contentious matter of analytic disclosures, Barbara once again draws our attention to the multiple dimensions of this issue and its embeddedness in the analyst's use of self. More specifically, this paper focuses on a disclosure that not only reveals personal information, it simultaneously divulges Barbara's confidential relationship with another. Certainly such a boundary crossing gives us serious pause for thought. Yet, Barbara, in daring to go where others seldom do, invites us to reconsider ourselves in terms of those “hot” moments of intimate encounter, those moments where aspects of ourselves feel so on the line that we find ourselves responding in ways we could never have imagined, let alone anticipated. Yet these are the very moments that often offer us our best chance at making a difference. In some way or other, we are both knowingly and unknowingly swept up by and thrust into these moments. But we have to be open to them—to recognize and be able to surrender to the moment that confronts us. These are the moments that tempt us to turn away, the quicksilver but complex moments demanding that we exercise the restraints of analytic responsibility while simultaneously inviting us toward freedom of imagination and curious engagement.

In what we have come to recognize as Barbara's forthright and openly sharing way, she details her revealing to her patient, Kate, that Kate's ailing analyst, Ariel, had at a much earlier time been Barbara's analysand.

Reply to Commentaries

Barbara Pizer EDD ABPP

Barbara Pizer

152 Brattle Street
Cambridge, MA

Barbara Pizer  

I hope that in the future, publishing a wider variety of written psychoanalytic communications will seem valuable to all of us.

—Donnel Stern (2005)

Our editor has taken a significant risk in publishing a paper and two discussions by authors who are all three intimately connected with one another. What potential did he seek to plumb? As I look back on my paper and consider these discussions, I am, in fact, shaken by my experience as I see it reflected in the eyes of two close friends.1 Surely it must have been a daunting task for them to have to publically reveal their actual “take” on clinical work reported by a personal colleague! But it seems that the result of Donnel Stern's risky experiment has uniquely opened me to new perceptions and understandings of Ariel, Kate, myself, and my respondents.

I find that Stern has succeeded, in vivo, in demonstrating the power of intersubjectivity to shape and reshape experience.

An interesting example of this power is embedded in the idea elaborated by both discussants, though never explicitly stated by me in the case, that my disclosure to Kate was “deliberate.” The term does appear, however, in an earlier paper (Pizer, 1997) in which I arbitrarily distinguish “deliberate disclosures” from “inadvertent” and “inescapable” ones—“de-liberate” implying the analyst's purposeful choice to convey information that might provide in a Winnicottian (Winnicott, 1969) sense, some “other-than-me substance” for the patient's use. What thoughts can I draw from the surprising realization that both Stuart and Hazel take my heart-in-mouth utterance to Kate as a deliberate act? This act, explicitly stated, is one that “I have never done before or ever wish to do again.” What blindness do my two trusted friends see in me?

1Stuart, my husband, is also my close friend.55

Bringing Theory to Life

A Review of Having a Life: Self-Pathology After Lacan by Lewis Kirshner. Hillsdale, NJ: Analytic Press, 2004, 157 pp.

Katherine Weissbourd PHD

Katherine Weissbourd

911 Western Avenue, Suite 507
Seattle, WA 98104

Katherine Weissbourd  

Sychoanalysts are becoming more pluralistic, working with multiple theories and using comparative studies to synthesize them. These studies do double duty. They highlight strengths and weaknesses in the theorists they discuss, and they demonstrate how close reading and critical thinking can lead to new ideas. Lewis Kirshner's Having a Life is an example of such a study. He integrates the contributions of Lacan with the more familiar work of Kohut and Winnicott. Where earlier writers might have held up each perspective as a separate point of view, Kirshner interweaves them, seeking commonalities and shared understandings. This is not as easy as it might seem; the writer must do justice to each of the thinkers, while also navigating the cross-currents that flow among them.

In this article I respond to Weber's commentary by amplifying some of my initial points. While our papers dwell on overlapping themes, I believe there are differences in emphasis. Weber is particularly concerned with the challenge of establishing a balance between arrogance and self-doubt. While I acknowledge the importance of this concern, I place greater emphasis on the transformative nature of a type of radical acceptance. Responding to Weber's paper has given me an opportunity to think in greater depth about the relationship between nonduality, acceptance and surrender, and to elaborate on the relevance for psychoanalysis of the Zen notion of perceiving suchness, that is, a type of surrender or “letting go” that allows one to experience the perfection of things as they are.

I quote this section of Stolorow's compelling poem for reasons that, as he tells, becomes apparent as we consider the intricate tapestry of the personal and conceptual threads he has woven together. It is a tapestry that tells a tale of many turnings—turning backward, turning inward, turning outward, forward, and moving ahead.

Coursing his way through his pain, horror, and the agonizing loss of his wife, Daphne, Stolorow takes us on his long journey through paralyzing trauma to the eventual opening of a space. A space that permitted the emergence of a qualitatively different grieving and, along with it, a sense of release, revitalization, and enhanced connection, as the temporal bridges between past and present began to achieve new purchase.

Through this personal journey, Stolorow demonstrates, in vivo, much of what the trauma literature has highlighted for us. He has documented many of these ideas in papers written at various points after Dede's death (Stolorow, 1999, 2003, 2004).

I am deeply appreciative of Hazel Ipp's beautiful discussion, which not only shows an exquisite grasp of the ideas in my article, but creatively and movingly expands on them as well. I have one quibble. I do not see myself as privileging language, although I do think language is extremely important in emotional life. Rather, I view linguisticality, relationality, and somatic affectivity as constitutive elements of a potential contextual whole, within which the sense of being can take form and flourish. If I privilege anything, it is contextuality—the contextuality of emotional experience, of unconsciousness, and of the sense of being.

Sandra Buechler addresses the realities of doing treatment in a postmodern age where the rule book has been thrown away and we are all left instead with our “subjectivities.” What, then, guides what we do? Buechler, much impressed with the literature on emotion, uses it to inform her personal experience with patients, and humanize the analytic process. She describes helping patients to be more aware of how events in their lives are related and how listening for and understanding the affect-loading for different events helps make these critical connections. An analyst at the William Alanson White Institute, Buechler credits Sullivan for directing her toward a way of listening that works, and she is inspired by Shakespeare in her focus on the human condition. She divides her book into chapters with tides rarely seen in analytic books. Her empathic orientation toward both members of the analytic dyad creates chapter titles like “Inspiring Hope,” “Kindness in Treatment,” and “Bearing Loss.”

If this sounds a bit sentimental, not to worry. Buechler is a romantic, but is also firmly grounded in reality. She explores the risks, pain, and loneliness of being a psychotherapist in a compelling way, demonstrating a rare combination of melancholy and exuberance. Fitting, perhaps, because so much of what she talks about is finding the right balance in all aspects of the treatment. When should we disclose, when shouldn't we? How do we decide which of many possible lines of inquiry to follow? How do we maintain our integrity? How do we bear the repeated losses when our patients terminate? This volume is filled with good, sound advice for therapists, and would make an excellent textbook.

Roger Frie

Roger Frie  

Why read Freud? In today's psychoanalytic environment, this question is often passed over. The era when Freud and psychoanalysis was perceived as cutting edge, even radical, appears to be long gone. More often than not, the turn to postmodernism can be read as an attempt to reinvigorate contemporary psychoanalysis with a sense of radicality, even subversiveness. What is often overlooked in the process is just how radical some of Freud's ideas actually were—and in some senses continue to be. By introducing the notion of the unconscious, Freud undermined the belief that we are in control of our actions, thoughts, and behaviors at all times. By exploring the nature of sexuality, particularly childhood sexuality, Freud shocked the general readership. And by debunking religious fervor as little more than a neurotic pastime, Freud presented an atheistic challenge to religious dogma. All of this was radical and remains topical to this day—if one takes the time to read Freud and discover just how inventive many of his ideas were.

Michael Thompson's innovative, engaging new book, The Ethic of Honesty, encourages us to go back and take another look at what Freud has to say. His interdisciplinary approach, attention to history, and detailed etymological analyses are a refreshing and necessary change to the status quo in much current psychoanalytic scholarship. Thompson's interest is not to reiterate Freud's tenets (about which certainly more than enough has been written) but to demonstrate the ways in which many of Freud's key ideas have been misread, misappropriated, and misinterpreted by competing groups of psychoanalysts. Successive generations of classical Freudians and ego psychologists have both praised Freud and actually criticized him for a lack of rigidity.

Robert Rodman's book is a tour de force of psychoanalytic sensibility and eloquent scholarship. The book is in effect a psychoanalytic Bildungsroman, that is, a reconstruction, critique, and intervention all in one. It is an example of what Erikson may have meant by “disciplined subjectivity,” rising to interpretive cunning.

Rodman, a psychoanalyst and “artist under oath,” as biographers have been called, sustains his narrative with sensitive fidelity to fact. Pirandello observed: “A fact is like a sock which won't stand up when it's empty. In order that it stand up one has to put into it the reason and feeling which have caused it to exist” (quoted by Wrightsman, 1994, p. 183.) Putting reason and feeling into the facts of Winnicott's life is like the colloquial “putting socks on a rooster.” “Negative capability” notwithstanding, the effort may be unavoidably paradoxical—a deep dialectical tease. There is little prescriptive fit in Rodman, and perhaps more of the “loving struggle” that Karl Jaspers conceived the writing of biography to be. Brett Kahr's preliminary work, D. W. Winnicott: A Biographical Portrait (1996) offers a clipped rendering of lively fact. Rodman's work is far more comprehensive. It is neither a “warts-and-all” biography, Stracheyesque (Lytton) in style, nor is it ironical combination of hagiography and pathography, but rather clinician on clinician in the play space of the scholar's cell.

Consider the clinical case presented by Sue Boland in her new book. She describes a young woman, Miss E., who grew up with a famous father and, to all appearances, in a perfect family, yet who was “a very unhappy little girl” (p. 20). Miss E experienced psychological conversion symptoms in the form of “frequent stomachaches” and frequently had to be excused from the dinner table. Soon, an obsessive fear began to torment her: she developed a fixed, terrifying belief that she “had appendicitis and was going to need an emergency appendectomy” (p. 28). It seems that this thought had its origin in her reading of Madeline, concerning a little French girl who was sent away “at a heartbreakingly early age” (p. 29) to a boarding school, where she had her appendix removed without so much as a visit from her parents. Madeleine was “all alone, without mother or father,” and this is just what the patient dreaded. She too was sent away to school. Her father she experienced as “awkward” and “irritable,” “preoccupied” with his career, “self-absorbed” (pp. 14-15). He traveled frequently, but even when at home, he frequently “disappeared” from family events. He was kind and attentive toward other children, and widely admired by others for his empathy, but for his own child he showed little concern. Miss E watched him hold the children of friends on his lap, but never was invited there herself. Her mother she experienced as absorbed in father's career much more than in her child. Indeed, mother expected her to be a perfectly behaved child and to appear exceedingly happy, and when she was not, mother's words and actions left no doubt that the girl was giving “the perfect family” a bad name; Miss E's duty was to feel good and be good in order to keep up the family image. Instead, she became a “misfit” (p. 67). She couldn't trust her parents, but she couldn't trust her own feelings either. All she knew was that “it was essential that I never say or do anything, or express any feeling, that even hinted that [her parents]… were not the ideal parents they so desperately wanted to be” (p. 103).

Christina Sekaer MD PHD

Christina Sekaer

80 Eighth Avenue, Suite 1305
New York NY 10011

Christina Sekaer  

“You are your synapses. They are who you are” says Joseph LeDoux in his book The Synaptic Self. He feels this neurological view of self is not an alternative to psychological, social, moral, aesthetic, or spiritual views of the self, but rather attempts to show how these selves are realized in the brain. LeDoux is a highly acclaimed neuroscientist whose work includes extensive research on the amygdala. He has contributed greatly to our understanding of fear and other emotional systems.

Psychoanalysts have defined and discussed the term “self” in different ways for many years. LeDoux defines the self as the totality of the living organism, physically, biologically, psychologically, socially, and culturally, more like the term “personality” (p. 330) rather than just the conscious self. Thus animals have selves, but only people have human self-awareness. The “synaptic self” exists in the synapses or connections between the nerve cells in the brain. The idea that our memories and indeed all aspects of our selves exist as synaptic changes distributed across our brains is, for many, a new way of thinking. What might a “synaptic self” look like? Visualizing my “self” as a pattern of connections formed by synapses in my brain is reminiscent of the mental shift I made growing up regarding money. As a child I knew my money consisted of coins in a piggy bank; now it exists as magnetic pulses distributed over a network of computers in banks across the globe.

To present the synaptic view of the self, LeDoux starts with a detailed discussion of how the brain works. A neuroscientist may find this a fine review of research on the brain, from molecular and anatomical to cognitive, emotional, and motivational studies in humans and animals. A psychoanalyst with no background in neuroscience may find the detail and depth of the neuroscience material difficult in some sections, but still follow the general ideas. The book thus approaches its stated aim: to be clear enough for the lay reader while also of interest to scientists.

Donnel B. Stern and Philip M. Bromberg, Co-Editors

Donnel Stern PHD

Donnel Stern

Donnel Stern  

Max Deutscher, Ph.D. and Rose Spiegel, M.D. founded Contemporary Psychoanalysis in 1964 and edited the journal until 1970. Since their tenure, however, the journal has always had a single Editor: Arthur H. Feiner, Ph.D., 1970-1995; Jay R. Greenberg, 1995-2001; and me, from 2002 to the present. With this issue, that trend changes, and in a very exciting and dramatic way. Philip M. Bromberg, Ph.D. and I will now be Joint Editors-in-Chief.

Philip Bromberg needs no introduction to psychoanalysts and dynamic psychotherapists, and he is well on his way to achieving a similar stature among traumatologists. In bringing the concepts of self-states and dissociation to the center of psychoanalytic discussion, he has not only made an enormous personal contribution, he has affected the very nature of psychoanalytic discourse about both mental functioning and clinical process. We ask different questions because of his work. Anyone who knows him, and probably anyone who has read him, is aware that his contribution is something special, something that he knows from the inside and that very few in the history of our field have known in the way he does. Contemporary Psychoanalysis, its Editorial Board, and its readers are truly fortunate. All of us look forward to the coming years with excitement. I myself, I have to say, am bursting with it. I also happen to know personally what a spectacular editor Philip is, because he has made my own papers much better than they could have been without his advice.

But I have to say that most marvelous thing about Philip's decision to join me in editing the journal is not his editorial expertise, despite my admiration of it. The most marvelous thing for me about our working together is what it's going to mean for me personally. After beginning as student and teacher thirty years ago, Philip and I have become good friends and close colleagues.

Editors' Note

Paul Russell, M. D. (1934-1996) was an unusually esteemed and influential teacher and supervisor in the Boston area. Yet, in Stuart Pizer's words, he “remained almost totally unpublished in his lifetime” (see Pizer in this issue, where he also details the few exceptions).

We are pleased to be able to offer in this issue of Contemporary Psychoanalysis two of Russell's previously unpublished papers. The papers are accompanied by introductions to the papers and to Russell's influence and body of work. These introductory essays are written by Barbara Pizer, Ed.D. and Stuart A. Pizer, Ph.D., who were Russell's students and supervisees and later close friends of Russell and his wife, Deborah. Russell's remaining unpublished papers, with the exception of the two that appear in this issue, are to be published this year in Smith College Studies in Social Work, Volume 76, Issues 1 and 2.

When the unpublished work of a deceased author is to be published, the choice must be made about whether to edit the work as it would have been edited if it had been submitted for publication by the author himself, or whether to let it stand as it was written. The justification for the latter position is that the author is not present to accept or reject changes. In this case, the decision was made by the author's widow, who preferred no editing at all; but that, it turns out, is also the course we would have chosen ourselves.

Some Thoughts on Trauma, Autobiography, and the Work of Collective Memory**

Elaine Freedgood PHD

Elaine Freedgood

Elaine Freedgood  

Trauma is antibiographical. Trauma separates its victims from them selves, and it separates them from the time in which subjectivity finds its story: its days, dates, and durations. When trauma survivors say, as they often do, that they have lost track of time at particular moments, we have come to understand that they are also saying that they have lost track of themselves. In Holocaust memoirs, time often dissolves in relation to unexplained, unpunctuated waiting. While waiting endlessly in the cold, while waiting for soup, while waiting for news, while waiting for death, one's own or someone else's, while waiting we lose time, ourselves, the world. The effort to reckon time in these memoirs is chronically unhinged by an unreckoning. We hear it in phrases like “it might have been hours, but it may have been days”; “it might have been weeks, but it may have been months.” A subjunctive relation to the duration of one's suffering makes it both overwhelming and beyond narration. One waits for a restoration of meaning, of human time, of the unhesitating, unconditional grammar of present, past and future, the language of definite duration. This is the ordinary grammar of autobiography: it is something we reflexively think of as “given,” but not “given” in the sense of “possible to take away.”

Trauma cannot be undone or reversed; it is not easily addressed, much less written down. Because trauma “is not a mere wound somewhere that can be healed or left alone. Trauma, rather, consumes the self. The trauma of trauma is that it does not have a beginning or end, no space from here to there, no time of before or after, and thus cannot allow any discourse that might address trauma” (Breithaupt, 2005). Trauma, then, cannot be narrated.

*There is, of course, an enormous literature on trauma and narrative that I do not address in this brief essay. I would not attempt to address the psychoanalytic bibliography. For an excellent review essay of some key works by humanists in what is now called “Trauma Studies,” see Berger, “Trauma and Literary Theory,” Contemporary Literature (1997).

[[RunningHead]]

Response to Anna Ornstein

Elaine Freedgood PHD

Elaine Freedgood

Elaine Freedgood  

The narration of trauma is a heroic accomplishment, not a baseline measure of the survival of a soul. It reassures those of us who have not yet been traumatized that we too might survive; it suggests that the world can make sense again, that fate can be restored to the fateless. In other words, the narration of trauma acts to preserve hope in the face of horror: it is a refusal of psychic death, individual and collective. People who cannot narrate trauma may be very much alive in every possible sense of the word, but not able to shape their experience into the very specific structure that is “narrative”: a chain of events that are linked in some causal formation, in which there is a sense of closure and, ideally, a closure that confers meaning.

Many events and experiences seem to refuse this structure. And many writers have, in turn, refused the limitations of narrative. Thomas Hardy is probably the most famous example of a writer who turned away from and against this form. After writing many novels that we now consider to be among the greatest of the nineteenth century, he abruptly and permanently stopped writing them after Jude the Obscure in 1896. He came to distrust narrative as a too-rigid container of human experience and turned to lyric poetry for the rest of his life: a distinctly nonnarrative form as he practiced it.

The particular consolation of narrative, I think, is that it restores the time in which ordinary living takes place; it suggests that the survivors of enormous trauma and tragedy can resume ordinary lives; it marks an end, a limit, to a certain intensity of horror. It recounts not only experience, but its containment, and to an extent suggested most powerfully in the very fact of its being written down, the mastery or refusal of the ruination that certain horrific experience seems all too capable of producing. I would like to end my response as I ended my earlier paper, with my gratitude to Sophia Richman and Anna Ornstein for their memoirs, and the work they do in helping us to understand the past and to face the future.

Seldom does one have the privilege of reviewing work as important and impressive as these volumes. Along with Schore's earlier work, Affect Regulation and the Origin of the Self, these two new collections constitute a trilogy of carefully crafted and researched papers. They also mark “a clarion call for a paradigm shift, both in psychiatry and in biology and in psychoanalytic psycho therapies.” The papers included in the two volumes were published during the past decade with newer material added. One cannot over-emphasize the significance of Schore's monumental creative labor.

Schore convincingly argues that it is self and personality, rather than consciousness, that are the outstanding issues in neuroscience. The development of self and personality is bound up with affect regulation during the first year of life when the infant is dependent on mother's auxiliary “self-object,” right-brain-mediated nonconscious “reading” of her infant's needs and regulatory capacity. Mother both soothes and excites within her infant's ability to cope without becoming traumatized. In other words, an attuned adaptive “good enough” functioning is essential for right-brain structural-functional development. The self-organization of the developing brain can only occur in the finely attuned relationship with another self, another brain.

According to Schore, Freud's unconscious and preconscious are right-brain based rather than in the lexical-semantic-motor dominant left hemisphere.

Roger Frie PHD Psy.D.

390 West End Avenue, Ste. 1G
New York, NY 10024

Roger Frie  

Jon Mills is a psychoanalyst and philosopher, president of the Canadian Psychological Association's Section on Psychoanalysis, and editor of Contemporary Psychoanalytic Studies, a book series with Rodopi Press. He has written and edited a number of important psychoanalytic books recently, and many of the central ideas contained in these works can be

685

traced to The Unconscious Abyss. The aim of Mills's book is interdisciplinary: to help psychoanalysts and philosophers alike appreciate Hegel's theory of mind and its ramifications for clinical work. This is an ambitious, scholarly project at which Mills succeeds admirably.

To some readers, the tide of this book may not seem inviting. After all, revisionist schools of psychoanalysis, particularly the interpersonal, inter-subjective, and relational, are not generally given to discussing the unconscious at any length. At the same time, some clinicians remain hesitant to jump into the waters of philosophical discourse. What makes Mills's book stand out is that it helps the psychoanalyst and interested reader understand current debates in psychoanalytic theory and practice in ways that are both clinically relevant and historically illustrative.

Mills's approach is two-fold. First, to explain how Hegel develops a theory of the unconscious that is central to his entire philosophy. Second, to show the relevance of Hegel's philosophy to psychoanalysis, both historically and contemporaneously. Since the latter is of more direct relevance to clinicians, I focus primarily on Hegel's anticipation of psychoanalysis, and on Mill's own theory of “process psychology.” To begin, however, I want to provide some biographical and philosophical background since Hegel today is no longer a commonly known figure.

The philosophy of Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel (1770-1831) is without doubt one of the most influential of the modern era. In contrast to continental Europe, the stature of philosophy as a discipline has suffered decline in contemporary North American society. Whereas Derrida or Habermas are sometimes considered household names in France or Germany, here the influence of individual philosophers is usually limited to the academy. By contrast, in nineteenth century Europe and America alike, philosophy was considered the pinnacle of learning. William James, after all, was both the founder of modern American psychology as well as a philosopher of great renown. Not surprisingly, the impact of Hegel's ideas on a range of disciplines beyond philosophy is well documented and simply cannot be underestimated.

To Expose or to Cover Up

Human Vulnerability in the Shadow of Death*

Peter Shabad PHD

Peter Shabad

7141 North Tripp Avenue
Lincolnwood, IL 60712

Peter Shabad  

This paper explores various implications of our shared human vulnerability as mortal beings. The degree to which we are open to or are closed off to our vulnerabilities has a profound effect on whether we address the ultimate frailty of human suffering with compassion or ruthlessness. The author considers how the “existential shame” of our helplessness before death is paralleled by the sense of shameful exposure we feel when being rebuffed by significant figures in our life. As a result of many experiences of rejected vulnerability, human beings tend to defensively cover up their vulnerabilities by using the state of being self-conscious as a means of bracing for disappointment. The state of being self-conscious is informed by a “morality of survival,” in which strength is good and weakness is bad. The morality of survival is a retroactive morality in which good and bad depend on the success or failure of outcome. The author then explores how the attempt to cover up one's shame as an individual may lead to conformity and the construction of social hierarchies between “us” and “them.” The author emphasizes the clinical importance of helping patients confront the shames they most fear. Finally, in contrast to the fear-based morality of survival, the author proposes an ethic of mutuality based on the interdependent acknowledgment of human frailties and the wish to be of compassionate use to another.

A Review of Jill Bellinson Children's Use of Board Games in Psychotherapy. Northvale, NJ: Jason Aronson, 2002. 184 pp.

Susan Warshaw EDD ABPP

Susan Warshaw

11 Riverside Drive, Suite 5
New York, NY 10023

Susan Warshaw  

The Title of this book suggests it is essentially a primer, a “how to” introduction to a topic that on first blush would not be at the top of the list for most practicing psychoanalysts. For those with an interest in child therapy, however, there is more to this book than its title suggests. In an

125

understated way, Bellinson introduces us to, and takes very definite positions on, some of the most historically controversial aspects of child treatment technique.

This deceptively simple book serves equally well as a text for a beginning child therapist and an easy read for the seasoned analyst who wants a glimpse into the consulting room of a senior child clinician. With great candor and a refreshing lack of jargon, Bellinson brings the reader into her play-therapy sessions, introducing us to her young patients and, through extensive clinical examples, provides an introduction to the real world of child work. Although she never fully states her theoretical perspective, we gain some sense as to what Bellinson believes is “therapeutic” with children in the throes of a developmental process.

The manifest and controversial subject matter of the book is the use of board games in child treatment. Historically, board games have been marginalized, if not banned from the play therapy rooms of many child analysts. Due to their rule-based, structured nature, their use was perceived as antithetical to the analytic process. Their presence was tolerated as a parameter. Bellinson joins a small group of analytic clinicians who have written affirmatively and instructively about their use of structured games (Loomis, 1964; Meeks, 1970, 2000; Krimendahl, 1998, 2000; Herman, 2000) as vehicles through which children can demonstrate and work through dynamic issues. She specifically states that the use of board games in the treatment of school-aged children is not only appropriate, but that children's very interest in such games is a developmental achievement and ought to be treated as such, and not interfered with by the analyst. Rather than viewing the use of structured games as necessary for the treatment of the more fragile child, way-stations to the “real” treatment, or manifestations of resistance to a deeper exploratory process, she embraces them as an age-appropriate expressive medium through which “latency” age children demonstrate their strengths, dynamic conflicts, defensive styles, and transferential relationships.

“Aerial Kiss Attack”: Affect Communication, Demystification, and Analytic Self-Disclosure

Discussion of Barbara Pizer

Stuart Pizer PHD ABPP

Stuart Pizer

152 Brattle Street
Cambridge, MA 02138

Stuart Pizer  

In a 1997 paper, “When the Analyst is Ill: Dimensions of Self-Disclo-sure,” in which she describes the decision to inform all of her patients of her breast cancer in 1994, Barbara articulates a framework for thinking about various analytic disclosures in different clinical contexts. While not intended as an exhaustive schema, Barbara's contribution sought to remind us that self-disclosure can be a disciplined dimension of our analytic function, even as it carries with it inherent responsibilities for its impact and consequences. Barbara defines three overlapping yet distinguishable dimensions of disclosure: “inescapable” disclosures, the naming of the elephant in the room; “inadvertent” disclosures, the spontaneous and unreflective enactment of an aspect of the analyst's subjectivity; and “deliberate” disclosures, the mindful choice of the analyst to share with the patient a feeling, a piece of information, a poem, a chain of thoughts, as a provision of usable “other-than-me substance.” Barbara is seeking to remind us of the ceaseless tensions and precarious balancing between freedom and accountability, spontaneity and constraint, in the analyst's disciplined clinical work.

Barbara's more recent paper describes her risks and rationales in venturing a deliberate self-disclosure to a patient under extraordinary circumstances. Here she reminds us of the complex and contradictory contingencies and principles with which the analyst must wrestle in both the urgent, emergent clinical moment and the personal reflections and analytic process that follow. It is indeed a bedeviling idea for us to contemplate that sometimes to not disclose may be as mystifying in the analysis, and as compelling toward collusive dissociations, as it can be in family life.

Anna Ornstein  

Belonging to two different disciplines (Dr. Freedgood is a scholar of literature; Dr. Richman is a psychoanalyst), the two authors approached the questions related to Memory, History and Autobiography from different perspectives. I shall discuss the two papers together, however, as this will permit me to integrate—to some degree, at least—the literary and historical perspectives on the one hand with that of the autobiographical one on the other. While Dr. Richman's paper is strictly autobiographical, Dr. Freedgood has undertaken the task of linking personal (autobiographical) memory to history.

My discussion is in four parts: (1) I reflect on some of the current views on autobiographical memory; (2) describe my views on “trauma” (3) briefly refer to the relationship between autobiographical and collective memory, and (4) give some examples of the way in which traumatic memories my become transformed into creative activity.

Autobiographical Memory

The clinical and theoretical significance of the recall of memories has undergone considerable changes in the course of the history of psychoanalysis. We no longer think of memory as fossilized remnants of a bygone past. Rather, when recalled, memories are frequently fragmented, elusive, and selective; this is particularly true for episodic1 memories that constitute the major part of autobiographical memory.

The author traces the development of ideas of self through the early and later intepersonalists and then in the work of relational theorists. She describes her own effort to explore subjective “dwelling places of self-experience,” a view that potentially overrides the intrapsychic-interpersonal dichotomy. The “political” implications of theoretical divergence between the interpersonalists and relational-ists are examined with an eye toward transcending them. Recommendations are offered for future efforts to theorize the nature of self.

David Mark  

discovery, co-creation, dissociation, projective identification, interpersonal, relational, multiple selves

For most of the twentieth century, the discovery of unconscious experience was a central goal in psychoanalysis. As postmodern currents gathered force, there has been a shift toward the co-creation, rather than discovery, of unconscious experience. Dissociative experiences that emerge in therapy are, in some sense, not previously known (and therefore could only have been created). Yet, they often feel like dramatic discoveries. A case is presented that illustrates how patient and therapist created a relationship in which (a) the therapist slowly lost a conflicted state and dissociated his own self-interest; (b) the patient participated in helping the therapist discover the version of himself he had become, which collapsed the dissociation and allowed his internal conflict to reemerge; (c) this created a new interpersonal context, both safer and more demanding for the patient, in which the live presence (and not merely, inferred existence) of her dissociated selves emerged. These selves had a transitional status in which the question of discovery and creation was “not to be asked.” Because they emerged nontraumatically, even playfully, these selves did not crowd out other “self-states,” thereby allowing the patient to think about these dissociated states.

Katie Gentile  

This paper describes a psychoanalytic exploration of eighteen years of one woman's diaries. These diaries document Hannah's struggle to come into being after a history of severe trauma and eating disorders. The diaries convey a detailed account of how the unspeakable, embodied remnants of sexual trauma become symbolized. Using her diaries as flexible transitional spaces, Hannah gradually begins playing with the structure of her text, creating bodies of herself and others within lists. Her use of lists within the diaries demonstrates that she develops the psychological capacities to differentiate and symbolize her abusive experiences only as she creates time. Integrating Loewald's (1980) concept of temporal linking, Winnicott's (1970, 1971) notion of psyche/soma development, and feminist criticism, this paper describes a theory of development where the analytic subject comes into being through the relational creation of time and space. This theory situates time as a unique and necessary space within which mind/body, self/other, and intrapsychic/culture are negotiated. Thus, this theory of time creates the potential space within which psychoanalytic and cultural subjectivities can be explored together. Hannah's use of lists illustrates this theory of temporal development.

Jon Frederickson

Jon Frederickson  

It is perhaps with some nostalgia that we look back upon a time when psychoanalysis could be understood as a relatively cohesive theory and body of knowledge. Yet today, as is well known, competing psychoanalytic theories often rest on incompatible formulations regarding the unconscious, theory of mind, analytic surface, transference, and therapeutic process. Some clinicians remain tied to one theoretical model, others try to draw from multiple theories but within a relational context, and still others, drawing from Kuhn, await a paradigm shift in theory.

John Fiscalini proposes such a paradigm: coparticipant inquiry. He claims that the controversies that plague psychoanalytic praxis result from differing conceptions “of the coparticipant psychoanalytic situation and its constituent processes of dyadic interactivity and psychic subjectivity” (p. 6). Fiscalini uses the term “co-participant inquiry” in three ways to describe: (1) the facts of the clinical situation, which are then interpreted in different ways by theorists; (2) a clinical stance; and (3) a philosophical statement about personhood and human relations.

Coparticipant inquiry as a clinical situation and stance is characterized by seven principles:

the analytic situation is an interpersonal field where the coparticipants influence each other, jointly shaping the unique course of the treatment.

analytic relatedness is a dialectic between interpersonal processes (intersubjectivity) and personal processes (unique individuality), and a dynamic relation between a personal, nonrelational self and an interpersonal self.

In this paper I present three collections of a patient's words and phrases that I arranged in a particular form. I discuss how I arranged the words in this way as I was struggling to get a sense of what felt “emotionally true” in my work with this patient and how this process helped me to grasp her use of dissociation. I draw on Gergen's work for a cultural perspective on dissociation, on Winnicott's concept of psychesoma dissociation, and on Goldberg's additions to Winnicott's theory. I show how the use of omnipotent, narcissistic structures may mask the use of dissociation (by patient and analyst) and make it quite an elusive phenomenon. My focus is on the process I went through, clinically and in my thinking and writing, as I discovered my own and my patient's dissociated use of mind and emotion and grappled with how to find a reassociation between these psychic functions and their somatic base.

Paul Russell  

When I was in training—and I suspect the same is true for some Df you—an article that appeared over and over again on required reading lists was a piece by Edward Bibring, entitled “Psychoanalysis and the Dynamic Psychotherapies”.1 In it, he said that for the dynamic psychotherapies, that is, any psychotherapy drawing on the fundamental principles of psychoanalysis, there were only five basic therapeutic procedures—five things one could do in one's capacity as a therapist. He ordered them in a hierarchy, proceeding from the more suggestive and manipulative to the more essentially and strictly psychoanalytic. In order, the five were: suggestion, abreaction, manipulation, clarification, and, the place at the top was occupied by interpretation.

Interpretation is understood as interpretation of wishes, most especially unconscious wishes. To cast the therapist's role is this manner amounted to a restatement of the assumptions of drive theory, following the model of a dynamic unconscious. However, putting the matter in this way provides every therapist with the opportunity to observe directly the powerfully organizing function performed by the capacity to wish. There is never a time when one cannot discover some more relevant, more accurate reply to the question “What do you really want?”

As with everything Bibring wrote, the article was very thoughtful, conceptually tight and written in a highly dense, compacted manner. It was an extremely slow read for me, and it left a long and lasting impression. I am only now deciding that I don't think I entirely agree. Exactly why, may take another 25 years to sort out. The closest I can come is to say is that interpretation is simply not what I think of myself as doing. This is especially so when what seem to be the critical parts of the treatment process are taking place. I don't mean to say that I don't interpret. I do. Probably more than I should. I do it, often, when I don't know what else to do. But, more and more, interpretation is not what I think of myself as doing as a therapist. I cannot quite find words that describe what I do think of myself as doing.

Using a case of Owen Renik's, the issue of self-disclosure, and, most importantly, a discussion of the effects of the analyst's concrete psychic and behavioral actions on the immediate analytic context, I outline an experiential-contex-tual perspective of psychoanalysis. I distinguish this perspective from traditional analytic perspectives that emphasize interpretation, the understanding of meaning, and clinical interventions based on a consensually validatable reality.

The perspective I present is clinically grounded in the analyst's utilization of emergent and unbidden experience that I see as arising from her or his unconscious embeddedness in the immediate clinical context. This experience appears to move on its own as a function of clinical contexts that continually change as a result of the analyst's ongoing psychic and behavioral actions. Working strongly from such experience can lead both to surprising speculations about what is going on in the treatment and to innovative ways in which the analyst might act.

In contrast, the traditional ways of working draw largely from the analyst's conscious and directed thoughts and feelings, which, in turn, are based on a more prescriptive and reality-based understanding of what is taking place with the patient and in the treatment in general. From an experiential-contextual perspective, the analyst's sense of knowing appears emergently and unbidden—almost as a free association—rather than as something the analyst actually “knows.”

Coparticipant Inquiry**

Analysis as Personal Encounter

John Fiscalini PHD

John Fiscalini

498 West End Avenue, 3B
New York, NY 10024

John Fiscalini  

coparticipation, inquiry, therapeutic action, living through, paradigm, analysis, mutuality, uniqueness

Two paradigms have dominated psychoanalytic praxis: the classical model that views the impersonal analyst as objective mirror, and the interpersonal-relational model that views the analyst as intersubjective participant-observer. A shift in psychoanalytic consciousness, however, has been taking place, giving rise to coparticipant inquiry, a third paradigm that integrates the individualistic emphasis of classical theory and the social focus of participant-observation, avoiding the reductionism of each. This new perspective, which is rooted in the radical teachings and clinical experiments of Sandor Ferenczi and the early writings of Benjamin Wolstein, presents a significantly different concept of analytic data, technique, and process, and a different perspective on the nature of analytic participation. This essay articulates the seven guiding principles of coparticipant inquiry and reviews their implications for such analytic issues as transferernce and countertransference analysis, defense analysis, the therapeutic role of immediate experience, the uses of self-disclosure, and the curative effects of the living through process. The clinical dialectics of the interpersonal and the personal dimensions of the coparticipant self are examined. The inherent mutuality, bidirectionality, psychic symmetry, egalitarianism and dyadic uniqueness of coparticipant inquiry and its implications for analytic work are examined. In all this, the unifying theme is that of psychoanalytic inquiry as a personal encounter.

The model of mind upon which Klein and Bion built their psychoanalytic theories profoundly limits an individual's access to the external world or other people. As a result, Klein and Bion posit the subject as imprisoned from the beginning of life in a solipsistic world of infantile phantasy. Such theories have paradoxically elevated the contents of the mind to a privileged status over perception, making what is in the mind even more “real” than the world as experienced, or relations with others. The mechanism of projective identification has been relied on to explain communication in the absence of a theory that permits anything we may today call “interaction.” Kleinian theory is contrasted with a relational orientation that emphasizes the primacy of immediate social relations in the constitution of the subject and as its source of freedom.

Optimally, the desired and feared mother of early childhood becomes transformed over time into an integrated whole object with whom one can both identify and disidentify. In this article I explore some of the implications of the Buddhist perspective on nonduality and acceptance for psychoanalytic practice. Nonduality is a mode of experiencing that breaks down the distinction between categories that are conventionally regarded as opposites (e.g., good versus bad, pure versus impure, sacred versus profane, heaven and hell). The Buddhist perspective on non-duality is that the natural human tendency to think about things in dualistic terms is at the heart of the problem and that wisdom is the ability to experience things nondualistically. As long as we distinguish between things as they should be in some idealized state versus things as they are, we are unable to be fully open to, and appreciate the present situation for what it has to offer. I attempt to convey a sense of the way in which the cultivation of a nondual perspective can lead to a radical and paradoxical perspective on the role of acceptance in the analytic process.

Clark Sugg  

Psychoanalysts are well aware of the tripartite structure of psychoanalytic education: personal analysis, supervision of control cases, and didactic course work. Most analysts would probably be surprised to learn, however, that at the same Budapest conference where Freud adumbrated this structure in the fall of 1918, he also made a commitment to clinics that would be under the same umbrella, if not actual roof, of the various psychoanalytic institutes. Furthermore, the clinics were to be supported financially by their respective institutes; patients would be seen on a sliding scale, ranging as low as zero. Psychoanalysis would thus become available to members of all social strata.

Freud's proclamation to start clinics did not fall on deaf ears. The number of participants who were in Budapest in late September and early October 1918 was large and reads like a “Who's Who” of early psychoanalysis. The list included Max Eitingon, Ernst Simmel, Eduard Hitschmann, and Sandor Ferenczi, Melanie Klein, Hanns Sachs, Sandor Rado, and Karl Abraham. All were instrumental in the founding of clinics, first in Berlin, then Vienna, followed by Paris, London, and Zagreb. Elizabeth Danto discovered at least twelve of these clinics. Danto's work provides us with until now a missing and important piece of scholarship. While some of the clinics fell victim to the Nazis by 1938, others, such as those in London and Paris, still function today.

This book is much more than a history of psychoanalytic clinics. It is a history of Red Vienna during the twenty-year period from 1918 to 1938 and the relationship of psychoanalysis to the larger political movement of the time. Freud maintained close relationships with socialists, including Ernst Simmel. Some of the psychoanalysts of the period, including Erich Fromm, identified themselves as Marxists.

Reply to Itzkowitz

John Fiscalini PHD

John Fiscalini  

I thank Dr. Itzkowitz for his thoughtful and thought-provoking discussion of my paper. Focusing on the concepts of coparticipant inquiry and the personal self, he adroitly surveys various facets of these two concepts and situates them in the history of psychoanalytic ideas, particularly in terms of their development within the Sullivanian and Frommian interpersonal traditions in psychoanalysis. Dr. Itzkowitz poses some important and interesting questions. To give his questions, many of which touch upon current controversies in psychoanalysis, the consideration they merit would require another paper, perhaps more.

So, in this reply, I briefly review Dr. Itzkowitz's most pressing questions and leave the others for another time. Before considering Dr. Itzkowitz's thoughts on coparticipant inquiry and the concept of the personal self, I would like to comment briefly on the seminal role of the Frommian and Sullivanian traditions in the evolution of coparticipant psychoanalysis. As I discuss elsewhere (Fiscalini, 2004; see the preface and chapter 3) and Dr. Itzkowitz elaborates in his discussion, coparticipant inquiry represents, in part, an integration of these contrasting analytic perspectives, incorporating Sullivan's (1940) operational focus on social adaptation and the consensual and communal in human relations and Fromm's (1947) individualistic emphasis on core-to-core relatedness, immediate experience, and personal encounter in the therapeutic situation.

Ironically enough, the Frommian analytic perspective, though important in the development of coparticipant inquiry, seems to have waned in its influence in contemporary interpersonal psychoanalysis, while Sullivan's star continues to shine brightly. Thus the humanistic or existentially oriented writings of such interpersonal theorists as Rollo May, Leslie Farber, Ernst Schachtel, or Erwin Singer, among others, are relatively neglected.

Sophia Richman  

I First Met Anna Ornstein twenty-five-years ago when I took her workshop in self psychology. At the time, I had no idea of the similarities in our backgrounds, for in those days we rarely spoke about our Holocaust past. The blanket of silence that had settled over the whole subject after the Second World War was just beginning to lift, so even if I had known about our common history, I doubt that it would have been a topic of conversation between us.

Now so many years later, I am discovering many things about this remarkable woman whose life is an affirmation of her views about resilience and strength in the wake of trauma. From her discussion of my paper, I can see how many ideas about this subject we share.

Dr. Ornstein takes issue as I do with those scientists and practitioners who perceive survivors as victims, inevitably damaged by traumatic events, and suffering from various degrees of psychopathology. In her discussion of my paper, also informed by her reading of my memoir, she points out that sometimes early experiences of exposure to traumatic circumstances can actually be a source of resourcefulness and creativity and lead to an enhanced capacity to grasp complex situations. It is a conclusion that resonates with my personal experience; as would be expected in the presence of a good self psychologist, I feel understood and recognized.

Moreover, I agree with Dr. Ornstein's observation that mental health professionals as a general rule have tended to view survivors in very limited and stereotyped ways. In recent years, even with the focus shifting from damage to resilience, I have noted that the concept of resilience is used to explain why survivors don't react with symptoms or syndromes, as if some special and unusual quality is necessary for people to cope effectively with adversity.

interpersonal, history, W.A. White Institute, ecumenism, politics, poetics, pragmatics

Interpersonalism, fifty years ago, was a radical departure from the Freudian position, both metapsychologically and politically. Indeed, it was radical enough to warrant apostasy and excommunication. I trace the vicissitudes of our outsiderness, both pro and con, up to our current achievement of genuine ecumenism. In general, the field has shifted from theoretical absolutism to a postmodern acceptance of multiple theories and truths, and, indeed, multiple selves. I suggest that we need to develop a vigilant dialectic of similarity and difference to avoid our past discordance and, what might well be worse, a well-intentioned but ultimately disastrous cooptation of our differences.

By my count, Michael Eigen has now published eleven books and scads of essays over a period of more than thirty years, making him one of the most prolific of analytic writers. He has created a body of work that spans enough time and territory to be read organically for its collective coherence. And that, I'm afraid, is the rub. The brilliant quirkiness of Eigen's individual efforts, tickling, teasing, provoking us around aspects of analytic-human experience, now present a greater challenge: In an age when psychologists in California are warned by their Licensing Board to “fear lawyers with knowledge of the research literature,” what are we to make of all this elaborated talk of mysticism, faith, dreamwork, and madness X? On September 21, 1897, Freud wrote a letter to his friend Wilhelm Fliess saying that he had changed his mind. Fliess' side of the correspondence has not been preserved, so we have no way of knowing what his reaction to this letter was, but I would be willing to bet that the latter-day readers of Freud's letters have pored over this particular piece of correspondence far more intensively than did Fliess himself, who by most accounts had his own preoccupations.

In this letter, Freud said that he no longer believed in his “neurotica”: that is, he no longer believed that sexual trauma played a major role in the etiology of neurosis. The September 1897 marker is quite arbitrary. His other letters show that he waffled; he was clearly loathe to give up the earlier theory. It is not hard to guess why: there was a clarity, a specificity, and an elegance to the trauma theory; it had its own self-contained theory of etiology, pathogenesis, epigenesis and the requisite therapy. For a man as ambitious and on-the-make as the early Freud, it must have been a bitter pill to give it up. Despite the apparent good spirits with which he gave voice to his new perspective in the 1897 letter, it still took him seven years more before he publicly recanted the trauma theory.

There are those who say that he had it right the first time. Jeffrey Mas-son1 would say that everything that came later was a massive retreat on Freud's part, a cop-out from facing the enormity of what he had known to begin with. Masson has a point. The most painful and difficult perception for anyone—and we all make assaults on truth to avoid it—is the perception of injury at the hands of a parent. But Masson's way of saying this is, to my mind, more assaultive to the truth, or at any rate, to the transitional objects we call truth, than is Freud's. Let me try to say why.

Survivors of tragedy are often robbed of their voice. Shame and fear following trauma encourage silence and a tendency to hide. Dissociation, initially a coping mechanism, leads to discontinuity and fragmentation and ultimately undermines one's sense of identity. Telling one's stoiy is an empowering experience that potentially restores a sense of continuity and wholeness.

The author, a child survivor of the Holocaust, a psychoanalyst, and the author of an award-winning memoir, draws on her personal experience to highlight various aspects of autobiographical narrative and its potential for facilitating the healing process.

Although relatively few psychoanalysts have written their memoirs, a number have used their own lives disguised as case material. Further, there is a current trend in clinical psychoanalysis toward greater personal expression and self-disclosure. The impact of analyst self-revelations on the therapeutic process has been researched by Dr. Richman and is further discussed in this presentation.

Billie Pivnick  

Gender-as-identity was long ago deconstructed by postmodernist theorists. Like Simon and Garfunkel's dangling conversation, identity is now played in syncopated time, and found—with melancholy sighs—on the borders of our lives. Front and center, gender instead has taken the lead. Shorn of unity, conceived discursively, it is likely to be characterized by separate and separated texts: “You read your Emily Dickinson, and I my Robert Frost.” Devoid of bodies, the genders may as well be “verses out of rhythm, couplets out of rhyme.” But to the question, “Is the theater really dead?” the answer is “No.” Gender, we're now told, is the original performance. Until now, the average relational analyst, schooled in the pitfalls of false-self relating, may have found this small comfort. Instead, many have “note[d] our place with bookmarkers that measure what we've lost.” With literary criticism and political considerations now imperative to gender study, we have been left to wonder, like the songwriters, “Can analysis be worthwhile?” A relational psychoanalytic approach to gender is not only worthwhile, suggests Adrienne Harris in her bold new book, but is essential for conceptualizing the paradox and multiplicity inherent in selfhood. Gender, she would argue, is actually coconstructed.

Harris's approach is thus a reply, of sorts, to psychoanalyst and linguist Bonnie Litowitz's (2002) question about contemporary psychoanalysis, but applied to gender: to what extent do our psychoanalytic notions of gender partake of “sexuality,” and to what degree have they been more influenced by what Litowitz calls “textuality”?

Russell, repetition, affect, negotiation, “crunch”, process, paradox

Paul Russell, who died ten years ago, had inspired and profoundly influenced thinking about clinical process among many analysts and therapists in the Boston area through his popular paper presentations at local programs, almost none of which were ever published or widely disseminated. My introductory essay (as does Barbara Pizer's) accompanies two of Russell's papers, printed in this issue in their original, unretouched form so that a wider audience may come into contact with Russell and discover the rich theoretical grounding, the clinical aptness, the prescient wisdom, in Russell's unconventional and direct writing. After offering a portrait of the extraordinary man Paul Russell was—brilliant, modest, humane, and generous—I underscore some of the essential ideas running through, and tacitly organizing, Russell's papers: affect and affective competence; the relational context for developing affective competence, and the implications for clinical process; trauma; repetition as crisis (“crunch”) and opportunity; paradox; negotiation; intimacy; loss and grieving.
